Steelman: The combination of row-level locking via FOR UPDATE and SKIP LOCKED allows any number of workers to safely dequeue distinct jobs without explicit coordination or external locking services.

Weakness: The pattern implicitly assumes the SELECT, job execution, and final DELETE/UPDATE all occur inside one short transaction whose lock is released only on commit; any implementation that performs non-trivial work (HTTP calls, external APIs, CPU-heavy computation) after the SELECT but before commit will hold locks for the full job duration.

Evidence: Under READ COMMITTED (the default), a worker that SELECTs a row then crashes or is OOM-killed before COMMIT causes immediate rollback and lock release; the next 100 ms poll by another worker will therefore obtain and re-execute the identical job, and any side effects already performed outside the transaction are not undone.

Falsification: Kill a worker after its SELECT returns a row but before its final COMMIT and verify whether the same job row is returned to a second worker within the next poll interval.

Verdict: critical MEDIUM

Steelman: Frequent polling plus SKIP LOCKED is claimed to give both low latency and high throughput even with dozens of workers.

Weakness: Each of the 50 workers issues a new transaction every 100 ms regardless of queue depth, producing a sustained minimum load of 500 transactions per second that each acquire snapshot and lock-manager resources; when job processing time exceeds roughly 200 ms the number of concurrent long-lived locks grows linearly with worker count, exhausting the lock table and causing queue-wide stalls.

Evidence: Postgres lock-manager memory scales with the product of concurrent locked rows and active snapshots; sustained polling under even moderate job latency therefore violates the unstated premise that each poll completes in <<100 ms and that lock churn remains negligible.

Falsification: Instrument lock-manager statistics (pg_locks, pg_stat_activity) while gradually increasing either worker count or mean job latency until throughput drops below arrival rate.

Verdict: high MEDIUM

Steelman: The database itself supplies durability, so jobs survive worker restarts or crashes.

Weakness: The scheme assumes that every worker maintains a dedicated, long-lived connection that survives the full fetch-to-commit window and that no connection pooler, proxy, or replica promotion will terminate the transaction mid-flight.

Evidence: On failover or pooler-enforced connection reset an in-flight transaction is aborted, the row is returned to the queue, and any partial external side effects already performed become duplicated work; nothing in the SELECT ... SKIP LOCKED pattern detects or prevents this.

Falsification: Trigger a connection reset (pg_terminate_backend or pooler timeout) on a worker between SELECT and COMMIT and observe whether the job is re-executed.

Verdict: high LOW

steelman: The pattern with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED allows safe concurrent claiming of jobs across workers without explicit locking code or central coordinator, and 100 ms polling plus 50 workers is presented as sufficient for typical throughput.

weakness: The approach provides no measurements or bounds on transaction duration, crash recovery semantics, or maximum job arrival rate, so it cannot rule out jobs being claimed then lost when a worker transaction aborts after the SELECT but before any status update.

evidence: A worker that obtains a row via SKIP LOCKED holds the lock only for its open transaction; any client disconnect, statement error, or explicit ROLLBACK releases the lock immediately, returning the row to the visible set for another worker while leaving the job record in its prior state. No checkpoint, advisory lock, or outbox table is described that would survive the failure window.

falsification: Run a 10-minute workload that injects random client disconnects after every successful SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and measure the fraction of jobs that complete zero or more than one time.

verdict: critical MEDIUM

steelman: Frequent polling with SKIP LOCKED is claimed to keep latency low while the lock granularity prevents duplicate work under normal conditions.

weakness: At 50 workers × 10 polls per second the system issues 500 SELECT statements per second against the same table; under any non-trivial job table size or concurrent DML this produces measurable lock-manager and snapshot overhead that grows with row count and connection count, yet no throughput or contention numbers are supplied.

evidence: Each FOR UPDATE acquires a per-tuple lock and forces a new snapshot; when the queue table exceeds a few hundred thousand rows or carries secondary indexes that must be considered, the fraction of time workers spend blocked on lock acquisition or waiting for snapshot reclamation rises sharply, turning the 100 ms interval into a source of sustained CPU and I/O load rather than idle time.

falsification: Execute pgbench with the exact SELECT statement at 500 queries per second while varying table cardinality from 10 k to 1 M rows and report both latency distribution and lock-wait events from pg_stat_activity.

verdict: high MEDIUM

steelman: The design assumes that once a job row is updated to a terminal state the change is durable and visible to all workers.

weakness: Any worker that performs the final UPDATE or DELETE inside a long transaction, or that relies on an asynchronous replication slot with lag, can expose a window in which the job is invisible to the original worker yet not yet committed or replicated, producing either loss on failover or re-processing on promotion.

evidence: PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default; a commit that marks a job complete may be lost on primary crash before the WAL record reaches the standby, and no synchronous_commit or quorum commit setting is stated.

falsification: Perform a controlled primary kill immediately after the worker issues COMMIT for a terminal-state update and observe whether the job reappears on the promoted standby.

verdict: high LOW

Target: Analyst A
steelman: The pattern with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED allows safe concurrent claiming of jobs across workers without explicit locking code or central coordinator, and 100 ms polling plus 50 workers is presented as sufficient for typical throughput.
weakness: The critique correctly identifies the post-SELECT abort window but assumes the only failure mode is client disconnect or explicit ROLLBACK; it overlooks the equally plausible case of a statement error inside the same transaction (e.g., constraint violation on a later UPDATE) that still releases the lock without advancing the job state.
evidence: Any error after the FOR UPDATE but before the status-changing statement aborts the transaction under default error handling, returning the row to the queue with no application-level progress recorded.
falsification: Instrument a worker to deliberately raise an error after a successful SELECT ... FOR UPDATE but before any UPDATE and measure duplicate executions.
verdict: critical MEDIUM

Target: Analyst A
steelman: Frequent polling with SKIP LOCKED is claimed to keep latency low while the lock granularity prevents duplicate work under normal conditions.
weakness: The 500 qps overhead argument treats every poll as independent and always hitting the lock manager, yet under low queue depth the queries frequently return zero rows after a cheap index scan; the real scaling cliff therefore occurs only when queue depth and worker count together keep many rows visibly locked, an interaction the stated evidence does not quantify.
evidence: When the visible job count drops below the number of concurrent workers, SKIP LOCKED short-circuits without acquiring per-tuple locks on already-claimed rows, so contention is data-dependent rather than purely poll-rate-dependent.
falsification: Repeat the pgbench test while keeping the number of unclaimed rows below 50 and report whether lock-wait events remain proportional to 500 qps.
verdict: high MEDIUM

Target: Analyst A
steelman: The design assumes that once a job row is updated to a terminal state the change is durable and visible to all workers.
weakness: The async-replication failure scenario presupposes that a standby will be promoted; the same terminal-state visibility problem arises even without failover when another worker's long-running transaction holds an ACCESS SHARE lock on the job table, blocking the visibility of the committed terminal row for an arbitrary period.
evidence: Any concurrent SELECT without FOR UPDATE still respects MVCC and can be blocked from seeing a newly committed row if an earlier snapshot is held open by a slow worker.
falsification: Hold one worker transaction open across a successful terminal COMMIT from another worker and verify delayed visibility of the completion.
